title: Knee Active Range of Motion | Basic AROM Assessment
purpose: Basic assessment of the four active knee movements: flexion, extension, and internal/external rotation of the tibia on the femur, while observing patellar tracking.
structure: Tibiofemoral joint; patella in the femoral trochlea (moves up and lateral in extension, down and medial in flexion).
procedure: Flexion: supine, bring the heel as far as possible toward the buttock. Extension: supine with straight legs, contract the quadriceps or push the knee into the bench so the heel lifts off. Rotation: sitting on the edge of the bench with legs hanging; palpate above the ankle to separate true tibiofemoral rotation from ankle inversion/eversion; foot outward = external rotation, inward = internal rotation.
positive: Not a positive/negative test: note range, symptoms and whether the patella tracks smoothly.
notes: Companion page to knee PROM. No references listed.

title: Knee Passive Range of Motion
purpose: Assess osteokinematic knee movements passively, measure range in degrees and evaluate end-feel when limited; includes patellar mobility.
structure: Tibiofemoral joint and patellofemoral joint. Reference values on the page: flexion 135°, extension 15°, internal rotation 20-30°, external rotation 30-40°.
procedure: Flexion: supine, hip flexed 90° and fixated at the distal femur, other hand on the distal tibia, flex maximally, assess end-feel. Extension: supine, leg flat, fixate the distal femur, grasp the distal tibia from medial (allows the screw-home mechanism) and extend. Rotation: supine, hip and knee 90°, lock the talocrural joint in maximal dorsiflexion and use the foot as lever for internal and external rotation. Patella: leg fully extended, glide medially with both thumbs, laterally with the index fingers, distally with index finger and thumb or the pisiform, proximally with index finger and thumb.
positive: Not a positive/negative test: compare range with reference values and the other side; note end-feel.
notes: Reliability: van Trijffel et al. 2010 systematic review found acceptable to excellent inter-rater reliability for knee flexion/extension by vision or goniometer; Mehta et al. 2017 found digital goniometers and smartphone inclinometers good to excellent and consistently superior to analog devices. The page's end-feel table is not in the API text. Reference values cited from Soucie 2011 and McKay 2017.

title: Knee Resisted Isometric Testing | Basic Strength Testing
purpose: Basic strength and pain-provocation testing of the knee complex: flexion, extension, plus ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion.
structure: Knee flexors and extensors; gastrocnemius (crosses the knee posteriorly, active in plantar flexion); ankle dorsiflexion moves the tibiofibular joint and stresses its supporting ligaments.
procedure: Flexion: supine, knee about 30° flexion, resistance above the ankle, patient pulls the heel toward the buttock. Extension: leg resting on the examiner's forearm, other hand above the ankle, patient extends. Dorsiflexion: knee 90° flexion, fixate, downward pressure on the dorsum of the foot, patient resists. Plantar flexion: resistance at the sole, patient resists.
positive: Pain and/or weakness during a resisted movement.
notes: Part of basic knee assessment with AROM and PROM. No references listed.

title: Myotomes Lower Limb | Peripheral Neurological Examination
purpose: Myotome strength testing of the lower limb to help identify the pathological disc level in suspected lumbar radiculopathy.
structure: Lumbosacral nerve roots: L2 hip flexion, L3 hip extension (as listed on the page), L4 tibialis anterior/ankle dorsiflexion, L5 extensor hallucis longus/great toe extension, S1 calf (repeated calf raises), S2 knee flexion (root pathology rare).
procedure: Patient supine; test each myotome and compare the affected with the unaffected side.
positive: Weakness (paresis) within a myotome compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: Al Nezari et al. 2013 systematic review/meta-analysis, 14 studies, lumbar disc herniation

notes: Positive or negative findings barely change post-test probability (weak clinical value), yet it remains the best physical-assessment tool available. SOURCE NOTE: the page lists L3 as hip extension; it does not comment on this. Companion pages: dermatomes and reflexes, lower and upper limb.

title: Atraumatic Knee Pain Differential Diagnosis | ITBS, PFPS, Jumper's Knee
purpose: Differentiate the three common overuse causes of atraumatic knee pain in active young people: patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS), iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS) and patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee).
structure: Patellofemoral joint, iliotibial band at the lateral femoral condyle, patellar tendon. Osteoarthritis and degenerative meniscus lesions are the more likely causes in older patients.
procedure: All three are diagnoses of exclusion (rule out ligamentous or muscular injury first); special tests perform weakly. Use the clinical presentation: pain location (ITBS = sharp, localized lateral pain at the femoral condyle; PFPS and patellar tendinopathy = anterior, possibly diffuse), typical age (ITBS and patellar tendinopathy in adults; PFPS also in adolescents, typical patient a teenage female runner), and pattern of onset (all overuse after a rapid load increase; ITBS usually sudden, PFPS insidious over weeks).
notes: The comparison table referred to on the page is an image not present in the API text. No references listed.

title: Radiographic Knee OA | Knee Osteoarthritis Signs & Symptoms
purpose: Clinical classification cluster for knee osteoarthritis (Altman et al. 1986) as an alternative to relying on Kellgren-Lawrence radiographic grading.
structure: Knee joint: subchondral bone (highly innervated, tender bony margins), osteophytes (bony enlargement), crepitus.
procedure: Knee pain plus the six items: age > 50 years; morning stiffness < 30 minutes; crepitus on range of motion (e.g. during a squat; bony crepitus like a creaky door versus common synovial popping); tenderness of bony margins; bony enlargement; no increase in temperature.
positive: 3 of 6 items positive, or 4 of 6 for higher specificity.

accuracy.source: Altman et al. 1986 (page rates high clinical value to rule out or confirm knee OA)

notes: Imaging correlates poorly with pain; 40% of patients in Altman's study were asymptomatic. Central sensitization and psychosocial factors matter; treatment via load management, strengthening, mobility and education. Page also cites Kim et al. 2015 (hip OA).

title: Ottawa Knee Rules | Knee Fractures
purpose: Clinical decision rule to identify which acute knee injuries need radiography.
structure: Knee: patella, fibular head, knee flexion, weight-bearing ability.
procedure: Order X-rays if any applies: age 55 or older; isolated tenderness of the patella; tenderness at the fibular head; inability to flex the knee to 90°; inability to walk four consecutive weight-bearing steps both immediately after injury and in the emergency department (limping is allowed).

accuracy.source: Stiell et al. 1995; Yao & Haque 2012; Cheung et al. 2013

notes: Comparable rule: Pittsburgh Decision Rule (more specific per Cheung et al. 2013).

title: Pittsburgh Decision Rule | Knee Fracture Screening
purpose: Clinical decision rule (1994) to decide which knee injuries need radiography and reduce unnecessary X-rays.
structure: Knee after fall or blunt trauma.
procedure: Mechanism of a fall or blunt trauma, combined with either inability to walk four full weight-bearing steps or age younger than 12 or older than 50 years → X-ray.

accuracy.sensitivity: 77-100% across evaluations; 100% for the stated rule
accuracy.specificity: 57-79% across evaluations; 79% for the stated rule

notes: Significantly more specific than the Ottawa knee rules in Cheung et al. 2013. The flow diagram on the page is an image not in the API text.

title: Brush / Stroke / Bulge Test for Knee Swelling
purpose: Detect minor knee joint effusion (also called stroke, bulge or swipe test).
structure: Knee joint capsule / suprapatellar pouch; medial and lateral parapatellar gutters.
procedure: Patient supine with the knee extended. Brush 2-3 times over the medial knee from distal to proximal, then with the other hand brush 2-3 times down the lateral side from proximal to distal.
positive: A wave of fluid appears and bulges on the medial-distal side of the knee.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Sturgill et al. 2009, inter-rater kappa 0.75 (agreement = same grade or one grade apart)

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value. Alternative: patellar tap / ballottement test.

title: Patellar Tap Test | Ballottement Test | Knee Swelling Assessment
purpose: Detect intra-articular knee effusion; helps localize the lesion (extra-articular swelling such as prepatellar bursitis or patellar tendonitis gives a negative test).
structure: Knee joint cavity, suprapatellar pouch, patella.
procedure: Patient supine with the leg fully extended. Stroke downward to the suprapatellar pouch and hold pressure; with the other hand stroke upward, stopping just below the patellar apex. While maintaining pressure, press the patella with one finger and feel whether it floats.
positive: The patella floats/taps against the femur, indicating fluid under it.

accuracy.source: Kastelein et al. 2009 (traumatic knee patients in general practice)

notes: A negative test moderately excludes effusion. Alternative: brush/stroke/bulge test.

title: Bounce Home Test | Intra-Articular Knee Pathology
purpose: Detect intra-articular pathology such as meniscus tears or loose bodies that limit or make painful full knee extension.
structure: Menisci, intra-articular loose bodies, joint effusion limiting terminal extension.
procedure: Patient supine. Cup the patient's heel, start with the knee fully flexed and let the leg passively drop into extension.
positive: Normal: the knee bounces home into full extension with a sharp endpoint. Incomplete extension or a rubbery end-feel with joint-line pain suggests a torn meniscus; a hard end-feel suggests intra-articular fragments/loose bodies.

accuracy.source: n/a: not evaluated in diagnostic accuracy studies as originally described (Malanga et al. 2003)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other meniscus tests: McMurray, joint line tenderness, duck walk/Childress, Apley's, Finochietto/jump sign, Thessaly.
